overview: This two-document file records U.S. intelligence concerning the September 1941 movements and activities of the Japanese merchant ships Heiyo Maru and Noto Maru at Manzanillo, Mexico. An October 22 covering letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmits a confidential memorandum to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle Jr.; the memorandum describes ship itineraries, passengers—including Japanese military and diplomatic personnel—mail and sealed diplomatic baggage, unusually restricted access to the Noto Maru, possible carriage of war materials to Peru, the repatriation of Japanese residents from Mexico amid fears of conflict with the United States, and shipments of bronze, rosin, petrolatum, dyes, and mercury. It also alleges that Mexican immigration authorities and officials at Manzanillo extended special courtesies to Japanese shipping.

subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hoover forwards a confidential memorandum concerning recent Japanese shipping activity at Manzanillo, Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends Berle a memorandum dated September 23, 1941, entitled “Japanese Ships Recently at Manzanillo, Mexico,” noting that its information came from a reliable confidential source. He states that the same information is being forwarded to Nelson A. Rockefeller, Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs. Copies are indicated for the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department, and the Director of Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Heiyo Maru and Noto Maru at Manzanillo
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation, based on a confidential source
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports the movements, passengers, mail, baggage, cargo, and official treatment of two Japanese merchant ships calling at Manzanillo in September 1941.
subfiles.summary: The Noto Maru arrived from Japan en route to Peru, carrying Captain H. Sato and taking aboard Colonel Katsuki Semi Sima and Captain Yamahi; it unloaded German aniline dyes and U.S.-addressed mail under unusually strict access controls and was suspected of transporting Japanese war materials. The Heiyo Maru arrived from South America and departed for Yokohama with mail, more than one hundred Japanese passengers, Nippon Yusen Kaisha and legation personnel, and four diplomatically sealed boxes. It also loaded bronze, rosin, and approximately 250 drums of petrolatum consigned by A. Z. Phillips, although Phillips’s mercury was not permitted aboard. The report characterizes Manzanillo as pro-Japanese and says General Enriquez instructed immigration officials to extend special courtesies to both vessels.

interest: The file offers a compact snapshot of American surveillance of Japanese maritime networks less than three months before Pearl Harbor. It is especially useful for connecting merchant shipping with diplomatic travel, international mail, strategic commodities, expatriate repatriation, and Mexican administrative cooperation. The memorandum also preserves the uncertainty characteristic of intelligence reporting: several significant claims—particularly the possible carriage of war materials and the motives of returning Japanese families—are explicitly speculative and derive from a confidential source.
